questions.q: A sudoers line reads: jsmith ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx. What do the four parts of that line represent?
options: Who is granted access, which host it applies on, which user the command runs as, and exactly what command is allowed
The file owner, the file group, the file permissions, and the file size
The username, the password, the shell, and the home directory
Four unrelated comments with no fixed meaning
questions.explain: Every sudoers line follows who where=(as whom) what — user/group, host, run-as identity, and allowed command list.

questions.q: What does the % prefix mean in a sudoers line like %sudo ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL?
options: It marks the name as a group, not an individual user
It means the rule only applies on 50% of logins
It is a comment character, so the line is ignored
It restricts the rule to percentage-based disk usage
questions.explain: A %-prefixed name in sudoers refers to a group; without the %, the name refers to a single user.

questions.q: Why does jsmith ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx follow the principle of least privilege?
options: It grants jsmith exactly one command as root and nothing else, instead of full ALL=(ALL) ALL access
It gives jsmith a shell as root with no restrictions
It removes jsmith's sudo access entirely
It only works if jsmith is also in the sudo group
questions.explain: The rule scopes the grant to a single command rather than handing out unrestricted root access.

questions.q: Why must /etc/sudoers always be edited with visudo instead of a plain text editor like nano?
options: visudo validates the file's syntax before saving, preventing a save that could lock out sudo for everyone
nano cannot open files located in /etc
visudo is required because /etc/sudoers is a binary file
There is no real difference — either tool is equally safe
questions.explain: A syntax error saved directly with a plain editor can break sudo entirely, and fixing it normally requires sudo — a real lockout risk visudo's validation prevents.

questions.q: Why does sudo require absolute paths (like /usr/bin/systemctl) in a sudoers command list instead of a bare command name?
options: It prevents an attacker from placing a malicious binary with the same name earlier in a user's $PATH and having sudo run it as root
Absolute paths run faster than relative ones
Bare command names are not valid Linux syntax
It has no security purpose, it is just a formatting convention
questions.explain: sudo deliberately ignores $PATH for privileged commands, closing off a path-hijacking attack.
